extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, press officers, journalists, and researchers interested in PR and media relations
extracted.subtask_short: writing press releases for media pickup
extracted.subtask_description: A practical evaluative framework for crafting press releases likely to be picked up and used by journalists; includes criteria that matter for both resource-rich and resource-poor actors and predictors of media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provides information of public interest (not just self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The release should provide information of public interest rather than merely promote the sender's self-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis emphasizes that releases succeeding in the 'PR democracy' provide public-interest information. For resource-rich actors, this means offering facts or context beyond promotional claims; for all senders, orient angle toward broader public relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has verifiable claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in the release should be verifiable by journalists and third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verifiability increases journalist uptake because it reduces fact-checking burden. Include sources, references, data points, and contactable experts to substantiate assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comes from a trusted source
rubrics_metrics.description: The sender's reputation and perceived reliability influence whether journalists use the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established institutions get repeated coverage; building and maintaining a reputation for reliability is crucial. Past reliability is a strong predictor of pickup—so avoid one-off misleading or exaggerated releases that can damage trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has a clear newsworthy angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The release must state a clear, newsworthy angle that explains why journalists and audiences should care now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crisp lead, explicit hook, and relevance to current events (topic resonance with the news cycle) increase pickup. Avoid vague or purely promotional headlines; tie the story to a concrete development, data point, or timely frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is accessible to journalists (no paywall, easy contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be able to access the content and contact sources without barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid paywalls, make contact information prominent, and provide press kits in usable formats. Speed and accessibility (fast response, easy-to-find materials) are advantages, especially for smaller groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provides multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Include photos, video, charts, or other assets to make the story wire-ready and easier to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information subsidies that are 'wire-ready' reduce newsroom workload. Polished multimedia increases likelihood of use, but should accompany substantive information (see anti-pattern: polish alone). Provide captions, high-resolution files, and embed-ready assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is responsive to journalist follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Press officers should answer queries promptly and be available for clarification or interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsiveness builds relationships and increases the chance of coverage; include direct contact lines and offer spokespeople for immediate follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintains long-term relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: PR activity should be oriented to sustaining ongoing, trust-based relations with journalists and outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'burn bridges' with a single bad release. Long-term credibility and reciprocity (regular helpful contacts, consistent reliability) are rewarded in coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledges legitimate counter-arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Good releases transparently address likely criticisms or limitations rather than conceal them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging plausible counterpoints increases credibility and makes the release more usable to journalists seeking balanced coverage; it signals good faith and reduces perception of manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doesn't manipulate but informs
rubrics_metrics.description: The release should aim to inform journalists and the public rather than manipulate perception through misleading framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical practice: prioritize accuracy and context. Avoid spin, selective omission of salient facts, or framing designed to mislead; such tactics harm long-term pickup and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness independent of source
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrinsic news value of the story matters aside from who sends it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even powerful sources need newsworthy material; a topic that resonates with the news cycle or has standalone public relevance can be picked up regardless of sender prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-source friendly
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should be structured so journalists can combine them with other sources and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide verifiable facts, identify additional sources, and avoid single-source spin so reporters can build multi-source stories; this increases usability across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of information subsidy (wire-ready, substantive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall quality of the packaged information—clarity, structure, supporting materials—affects uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis notes information subsidies reduce journalists' workload; high-quality, well-structured, easily usable copy and assets increase pick-up. However, substantive quality must accompany polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source institutional power
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional resources and power (e.g., corporations, major unions) influence coverage likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource-rich actors often dominate coverage because they can produce higher volumes of polished subsidies and have established reputations. Modelers should include institutional power as a predictor while noting it can be counterbalanced by strong angles from smaller actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past reliability (reputation as reliable source)
rubrics_metrics.description: History of accurate, useful communications by a source influences journalists' trust and propensity to use future releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track record matters: reliable past behavior increases pickup; inconsistency or once-dishonest communications reduce future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal journalist relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct relationships between PR practitioners/activists and journalists influence distribution and pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal rapport, trust, and informal lines of contact are especially important for resource-poor groups. Cultivate relationships through responsiveness, helpfulness, and consistent provision of usable information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic resonance with current news cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Release topics that align with issues already on journalists' agendas are more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie your story to ongoing narratives, anniversaries, or emergent events to increase relevance. Timing and framing for the news cycle matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting precision
rubrics_metrics.description: How precisely the release is targeted to the right reporters/outlets affects pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send to journalists who cover the beat, tailor pitches, and propose story angles suited to each outlet; broad shotgun distributions are less effective than precise targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive offered
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering an exclusive to a single outlet can increase the probability of coverage by that outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusives can be valuable bargaining chips; use them strategically when resources or story uniqueness justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic voice over polish (advantage for resource-poor groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller or resource-poor groups gain by using authentic, expert, or passionate voices rather than purely polished PR copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis finds that one passionate person or niche expertise can rival corporate teams; emphasize authenticity, firsthand perspective, and accessible spokespeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niche expertise valued
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized knowledge or unique access increases a release's utility to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide expert contacts, unique data, or lived-experience perspectives that journalists can't easily obtain elsewhere; expertise can substitute for institutional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and accessibility advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Being fast to respond and making materials easy to use confers advantage, especially for smaller actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid availability of spokespeople, quick follow-ups, and readily downloadable assets increase the chance of uptake in tight deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modern tools (social media) as distribution/support
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveraging social media and modern communication tools complements traditional press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social platforms can amplify reach, create hooks for journalists, and allow resource-poor groups to bypass some gatekeeping—use them in coordination with journalist-facing materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish alone (without substance) is a weak predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: High production polish without substantive, newsworthy content does not reliably predict pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis identifies polish as a 'less powerful predictor'—wire-ready design helps, but content quality and news value are more important. Beware over-relying on formatting or stylistic gloss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution volume alone is a weak predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending a large number of releases or broad distribution lists by itself does not guarantee coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volume should be coupled with targeting, quality, and relevance; bulk distribution without a strong angle or source credibility is unlikely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing budget / PR spend is a weak predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a large PR or marketing budget does not on its own ensure media pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional resources help, but journalists respond more to verifiability, newsworthiness, and relationships than to how much was spent producing a release.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated polish is a weak predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmetic improvements from AI generation/rewrites without substantive new information do not meaningfully increase pickup likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis flags 'AI-generated polish' as a less powerful predictor; prioritize original, verifiable content and credible sources over machine-polished prose.
